title: Japan Accommodation Types Explained (Ryokan, Hotels, Capsules & More)
excerpt: Ryokan, business hotels, capsule hotels, minshuku — Japan has lodging styles you won't find at home. Here's what each is and who it suits.
content:
Japan offers lodging styles that go well beyond the standard hotel, and understanding them helps you pick the right mix for your trip. Here's a rundown of the main types and who each suits.

Western-style hotels

Familiar international and Japanese hotel brands operate across the cities, from luxury towers to mid-range chains. Rooms are comfortable and predictable, with English-speaking staff at larger properties. A safe choice if you want zero surprises, especially for your first night after a long flight.

Business hotels

Business hotels are Japan's mid-range workhorse — compact, clean, efficient rooms at reasonable prices, often near train stations. Rooms run small by American standards but are well designed and have everything you need. Excellent value for travelers who'll be out exploring most of the day and just need a good base to sleep.

Ryokan

A ryokan is a traditional Japanese inn — tatami-mat floors, futon bedding, often a shared or private hot-spring bath, and frequently a multi-course dinner and breakfast included. Staying in one is a cultural experience in itself, not just a place to sleep. They range from simple to extremely luxurious. Worth doing at least one night, ideally in an onsen town or Kyoto.

Minshuku and guesthouses

A minshuku is a family-run guesthouse, a more casual and budget-friendly cousin of the ryokan, often with home-cooked meals and a personal touch. Modern guesthouses and hostels are also widespread, popular with younger and budget travelers, and a good way to meet people.

Capsule hotels

The famously Japanese capsule hotel offers a single sleeping pod in a stack, with shared bathrooms and lounges. They're inexpensive, surprisingly comfortable for a night, and a fun novelty — though tight on space and not ideal for those who feel claustrophobic. Many are gender-separated.

Temple lodging (shukubo)

At some temples, particularly in places like Koyasan, you can stay overnight in temple lodging, sharing the monks' simple vegetarian meals and sometimes morning prayers. It's a serene, unusual experience for travelers seeking something contemplative.

How to mix them

A common approach for first-timers: business or Western hotels in the big cities for convenience, plus one or two nights in a ryokan — especially in an onsen town — for the traditional experience. That blend gives you comfort where you need it and culture where it counts. Whatever you choose, book early for cherry blossom and fall foliage season, when the best places fill up fast.

title: Best Areas to Stay in Japan: A First-Timer's Overview
excerpt: Where should you base yourself in Japan? A high-level guide to choosing your bases across Tokyo, Kyoto, and beyond for a first trip.
content:
On a first trip to Japan, where you base yourself is mostly a question of which cities you build your trip around — and for the classic first visit, that means Tokyo and Kyoto, with the right neighborhood in each. Here's the high-level view.

Tokyo: pick a hub on the loop

In Tokyo, aim for a neighborhood on or near the JR Yamanote loop so trains reach everything easily. Shinjuku is the do-everything all-rounder, Shibuya is youthful and central to the action, and Asakusa offers traditional charm and better value on the eastern side. Ginza is the upscale, quieter option. Any of these makes a strong base.

Kyoto: atmosphere vs convenience

In Kyoto, the choice is between charm and connectivity. Gion and Higashiyama give you the postcard old-Kyoto atmosphere within walking distance of major temples. The Kyoto Station area is the practical hub for transport and day trips. Downtown splits the difference, and Arashiyama trades convenience for scenery and calm.

Should you add other cities?

For one week, basing in just Tokyo and Kyoto — with day trips to places like Hakone and Nara — keeps things simple and covers the essentials. With more time, Osaka makes a great base for the Kansai region and its food scene, and is close enough to Kyoto that some travelers even base in one and day-trip to the other. Farther trips might add a night in an onsen town or in Hiroshima.

A simple rule for first-timers

Don't over-split your trip. Each city change costs you a half-day in packing, transit, and re-settling. Two well-chosen bases (Tokyo, then Kyoto) for a week, or three for two weeks, beats hopping between five hotels. Pick central, well-connected neighborhoods, and use Japan's excellent trains for day trips rather than relocating constantly.

Booking tips

Japan's most desirable accommodations — especially ryokan and well-located city hotels — book out early in peak seasons. Decide your bases, then reserve as far ahead as you can for spring and autumn travel. Comparing options and prices early for your specific dates is the best way to lock in a good spot.

title: Booking Hotels in Japan: Tips for American Travelers
excerpt: Small rooms, early booking, and unfamiliar lodging types — here's what American travelers should know before booking accommodation in Japan.
content:
Booking accommodation in Japan is straightforward, but a few things work differently than they do at home. Knowing them ahead of time helps you book smart and avoid surprises.

Rooms are smaller than you expect

Japanese hotel rooms, especially business hotels in cities, are compact by American standards. This is normal and not a sign of a bad hotel — space is at a premium. If room size matters to you, look at the listed square meters and consider paying up for a larger room or a Western chain. For most travelers who are out all day, the efficient smaller rooms are perfectly comfortable.

Book early for peak seasons

The single most important tip: reserve well ahead for cherry blossom season (late March–April) and fall foliage (October–November). The best-located and best-value places sell out months in advance, and prices climb. If your dates fall in these windows, book as soon as your plans firm up.

Location near a station matters most

In Japan's transit-based cities, proximity to a train or subway station is worth more than almost any amenity. A hotel a few minutes from a station saves you time every single day. Prioritize that over things like a big lobby or pool you won't use.

Understand what's included

Breakfast is often optional and added to the rate — Japanese hotel breakfasts can be excellent. Ryokan rates frequently include dinner and breakfast, which makes their higher price more reasonable than it first looks. Always check what the rate covers before comparing.

Practical booking notes

  • Major international booking platforms work well in Japan and list everything from capsules to luxury ryokan, usually with English support.
  • Check-in times can be strict, and many places ask for passport details at check-in for foreign guests — normal procedure.
  • Some traditional ryokan have set meal and bath times; read the details so you're not caught out.
  • There's no tipping, including at hotels.

Consider one special stay

Beyond your practical city hotels, consider booking one memorable night — a ryokan in an onsen town, a machiya townhouse in Kyoto, or even a capsule hotel for the novelty. It adds texture to the trip. Compare options and prices for your dates early, and you'll get both the convenience and the experience you want.

title: What Is a Ryokan? A First-Timer's Guide to Japanese Inns
excerpt: A ryokan is a traditional Japanese inn — tatami, futons, hot-spring baths, and elaborate meals. Here's what to expect and how to enjoy your stay.
content:
A ryokan is a traditional Japanese inn, and staying in one is one of the most memorable things you can do on a trip to Japan. It's less a hotel than a cultural experience — a window into traditional hospitality. Here's what to expect on your first stay.

What a ryokan is

Ryokan date back centuries and center on traditional Japanese aesthetics and hospitality. Rooms typically feature tatami-mat floors, sliding paper screens, low furniture, and futon bedding laid out on the floor (often by staff in the evening). Many ryokan have hot-spring baths, and meals are usually a highlight. They range from simple family-run inns to opulent luxury retreats.

What's usually included

Most ryokan stays include dinner and breakfast, and the dinner is often a multi-course kaiseki meal — an artful procession of seasonal local dishes. This is a big part of the experience and a reason the price is higher than a basic hotel; you're paying for the meals and service, not just the room. Check whether meals are included when you book.

The typical flow of a stay

On arrival you'll usually remove your shoes at the entrance and change into provided slippers. You'll often be given a yukata (a casual cotton robe) to wear around the inn, and at onsen ryokan, to and from the baths. Dinner is frequently served at a set time, either in your room or a dining area. While you eat, staff may lay out your futon. Breakfast follows in the morning.

Etiquette basics

  • Take your shoes off where indicated and use the slippers provided (and separate toilet slippers where present).
  • Wear the yukata as shown — generally left side over right.
  • Be quiet and respectful; ryokan are tranquil places.
  • If there's a shared bath, follow onsen etiquette (wash before entering, no swimsuits).
  • There's no tipping.

Who should stay in one

A ryokan suits any traveler curious about traditional Japan, and it's especially magical in an onsen town where you can soak in hot springs, or in Kyoto where the setting matches the culture. Even one night makes a trip more memorable. The trade-off is less privacy and flexibility than a hotel, and the floor-futon style isn't for everyone — but most first-timers find it a highlight.

Booking

Ryokan, especially the well-regarded ones in popular onsen towns, book up early in peak seasons. If a traditional stay is on your list, reserve ahead and check exactly what's included. It's worth the planning for an experience you can't get anywhere else.

title: Onsen Etiquette: How to Use a Japanese Hot Spring
excerpt: Japan's hot-spring baths have clear rules — wash first, no swimsuits, no towels in the water. Here's how to enjoy an onsen respectfully as a first-timer.
content:
An onsen — a natural hot-spring bath — is one of Japan's great pleasures, but the etiquette can feel intimidating the first time, especially for Americans unused to communal bathing. The rules are simple once you know them, and following them shows respect. Here's how it works.

The basics: wash before you soak

The single most important rule: you wash thoroughly before entering the bath. Onsen are for soaking in clean water, not for cleaning yourself. You'll find washing stations — usually a stool, a handheld shower, and toiletries — where you scrub down and rinse completely before getting into the communal bath. The bath water is shared and kept clean by everyone washing first.

No swimsuits — bathing is nude

Traditional onsen are enjoyed nude. Swimsuits are not worn in the baths. Baths are almost always gender-separated, so you'll be among others of the same gender. This is completely normal and matter-of-fact in Japan; nobody is paying attention to you. If communal nude bathing isn't for you, look for ryokan with private baths (kashikiri) you can book.

The small towel

You'll typically have a small towel. Use it for modesty walking around and for washing, but don't put it in the bath water — people usually fold it and rest it on their head or set it at the edge. Bring it back out when you leave to dry off before re-entering the changing area.

Other key rules

  • Tie up long hair so it doesn't touch the water.
  • Don't swim, splash, or be loud — onsen are for quiet relaxation.
  • Rinse off again after soaking if you like, but many leave the mineral water on the skin.
  • Drink water and don't overdo it — the hot water can be intense; step out if you feel lightheaded.
  • No phones or cameras in the bathing area, for everyone's privacy.

A note on tattoos

Some onsen restrict guests with visible tattoos, due to historical associations. Policies vary widely and many places are increasingly relaxed, especially in tourist areas, and some allow covering small tattoos with a patch or offer private baths. Because this varies by establishment and changes over time, it's worth checking the specific onsen's current policy ahead if you have tattoos — more on that in our dedicated guide.

Relax and enjoy

Once you've got the wash-first, no-swimsuit, towel-out-of-the-water basics down, an onsen is pure bliss — especially outdoors in a scenic setting. Locals are forgiving of visitors making an honest effort, so don't be nervous. It's an experience worth seeking out at least once.

title: Best Onsen Towns Near Tokyo and Kyoto
excerpt: Want a hot-spring getaway without going far? Here are the most accessible onsen towns from Tokyo and Kyoto for a first-timer's soak.
content:
You don't have to venture deep into the mountains to experience an onsen (hot spring) on a first trip. Several classic hot-spring areas sit within easy reach of Tokyo and the Kansai region, perfect for an overnight ryokan stay or even a day visit. Here are the most accessible options.

Near Tokyo

Hakone

Hakone is the go-to hot-spring escape from Tokyo — close, scenic, and packed with onsen ryokan, with the bonus of Mt Fuji views on clear days and a fun loop of mountain railways, ropeways, and a lake. It's the easiest and most popular choice for combining hot springs with sightseeing, and works as an overnight or even a long day trip.

Other options reachable from Tokyo

Beyond Hakone, areas in the mountains north and west of Tokyo are known for their hot springs and traditional atmosphere, offering a more rustic, less touristy feel. These take a bit longer to reach but reward you with classic onsen-town charm — wooden inns, steaming baths, and quiet streets. If you have time for an overnight and want something more off the beaten path than Hakone, they're worth considering.

Near Kyoto and Osaka

Kinosaki Onsen

From the Kansai region, Kinosaki Onsen is a beloved hot-spring town famous for its picturesque willow-lined canal and the tradition of strolling between several public bathhouses in your yukata and wooden sandals. It's a postcard-perfect onsen experience and a popular overnight trip from Kyoto or Osaka, though it's a couple of hours away by train.

Closer soaks

There are also hot-spring options closer to Kyoto and Osaka for those short on time, including areas reachable within a shorter ride. For a first trip focused on Kyoto, many travelers simply book a ryokan with its own onsen bath rather than traveling to a dedicated hot-spring town.

Day trip or overnight?

To truly enjoy an onsen town, an overnight stay in a ryokan is ideal — you get the evening and morning soaks, the kaiseki dinner, and the relaxed pace that makes these places special. But if time is tight, somewhere like Hakone can be done as a day trip with a public bath visit. Either way, build in enough time to actually slow down — rushing an onsen defeats the purpose.

Booking ahead

Onsen ryokan in popular towns fill quickly, especially on weekends and in peak seasons. If a hot-spring night is on your itinerary, reserve early and check what meals and baths are included. Confirm current access details and travel times for your specific dates when you book.

title: Tattoos and Onsen: What Travelers Need to Know
excerpt: Tattoos can complicate onsen visits in Japan, but options exist. Here's the situation and how tattooed travelers can still enjoy a hot spring.
content:
If you have tattoos and want to experience a Japanese onsen, it's worth understanding the situation ahead of time. Tattoos can complicate hot-spring visits in Japan, but there are good workarounds, and attitudes are shifting. Here's what to know.

Why tattoos are an issue

Historically, tattoos in Japan carried associations with organized crime, and as a result many onsen, public baths, pools, and gyms adopted rules barring guests with visible tattoos. These rules were aimed at that association rather than at foreign tourists, but they can apply to everyone regardless of what the tattoo is. So a tattoo that's unremarkable at home may run into a posted no-tattoo policy at a Japanese bath.

The situation is changing

Attitudes are gradually relaxing, especially with more international visitors. Many establishments — particularly in tourist-heavy areas and newer facilities — are more flexible than they used to be, and some have dropped tattoo restrictions entirely. But policies vary enormously from place to place, and there's no single national rule. The only reliable approach is to check the specific establishment's current policy.

Your options as a tattooed traveler

  • Book a private bath. Many ryokan offer private or family baths (kashikiri) you can reserve, or rooms with a private onsen bath. This sidesteps the issue entirely and is the most reliable solution.
  • Cover small tattoos. For small tattoos, a waterproof cover patch or bandage is sometimes accepted — ask the establishment first, as this isn't universally allowed.
  • Find tattoo-friendly onsen. A growing number of onsen explicitly welcome tattoos. It's worth seeking these out if you want the communal experience.
  • Ask ahead. When booking a ryokan or planning an onsen visit, simply ask about their tattoo policy in advance so there are no surprises.

Be respectful either way

If a place has a no-tattoo policy, respect it rather than trying to hide a large tattoo and risking an awkward situation. There are enough tattoo-friendly and private options that you don't need to push against the rules. With a little planning, having tattoos doesn't have to mean missing out on one of Japan's signature experiences.

Confirm before you go

Because tattoo policies differ by establishment and continue to evolve, treat any specific guidance as a starting point and confirm the current rules with your chosen onsen or ryokan when you book. A quick question ahead of time saves disappointment at the door.

title: Where to Stay in Osaka: Best Areas for Visitors
excerpt: Namba, Umeda, or near the castle? Here's how Osaka's main areas compare for first-time visitors looking for a base in Japan's food capital.
content:
Osaka makes a great base for exploring the Kansai region and its legendary food scene, and it's well connected to Kyoto and Nara. Where you stay comes down to whether you want to be in the buzzing south, the polished north, or somewhere quieter. Here's the overview.

Namba and Minami (the south)

Namba and the surrounding Minami ("south") area are the heart of Osaka's famous nightlife and food scene, including the neon-lit Dotonbori district. Staying here puts you in the thick of the street food, shopping, and energy that Osaka is known for, with great transport links. It's the top choice for first-timers who want to experience Osaka's lively side and eat their way through the city. The trade-off is noise and crowds.

Umeda and Kita (the north)

Umeda, in the Kita ("north") area, is Osaka's polished business and shopping hub, centered on a massive transport interchange with connections everywhere, including to Kyoto and the airport. It's more upscale and a bit calmer than Namba at night, with department stores, restaurants, and easy access. A strong pick if you value transport convenience and a more refined base.

Near Osaka Castle and elsewhere

Areas around Osaka Castle and other neighborhoods offer quieter, sometimes better-value stays while still being well connected by the city's loop line and subway. These suit travelers who want a calmer base and don't mind a short ride to the action.

Which to choose

For first-time visitors who want Osaka's signature food-and-nightlife energy, Namba/Minami is the classic choice. For transport convenience and a quieter, more upscale feel, choose Umeda/Kita. Both connect easily to Kyoto, so Osaka can even serve as your Kansai base with day trips out.

Booking tips

Osaka is a popular and busy city, so book ahead in peak seasons and prioritize a location near a subway or loop-line station for easy movement. Compare options and prices for your dates early to secure a well-placed spot in your preferred area.
